text.p: On overnight commodity markets, gold prices jumped on resilient support at the US$350 per ounce level and positive comments from funds.
Copper prices dipped slightly in further reaction from the strong rise on Friday.
Oil prices sagged on ample supply, while wheat closed higher in Chicago on a rally in soybean prices
The CRB Index closed up 1.82 points at 247.19.
Trading was subdued on the London Metal Exchange (LME) as copper led other base metals lower.

Copper futures eased in thin volume to close at $2,358 per tonne, compared to $2,389 on Friday. Traders said buying interest was sketchy in the wake of Friday's explosive rally which ended in a sell-off and a price plunge at the close.

Aluminium mirrored copper's bearish tone, and continued its weakness after a smaller than expected warehouse stock fall of 1,800 tonnes on Friday. LME three-month contracts closed at $1,657, down from $1,674 On Friday.

Copper dealers were watching for signs of China entering the market after the China Daily's Business Weekly said on Sunday that China's demand for copper would reach 1.2 million tonnes in 1997. The country produced over 900,000 tonnes of the red metal last year.
But Chinese traders ruled out any activity in the immediate future, saying prices were too high to justify buying.
A Shanghai Metal Exchange source said sky-high world copper prices were not supported by fundamentals.

"I don't really see any support for $2,400," he said. "If the price can go above $2,400 a tonne and stay there for a decent period, that would indicate some support, but I think the funds are under pressure to sell."

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed higher on a strong rally in the soybean complex, traders said. Support came from news the European Union may wrap up soft wheat exports from the 1996-97 campaign before the traditional end-April deadline.
But export sources said EU wheat values remain below U.S. prices.
Also the market found underlying support on evidence of strong stopping of the deliveries posted against the March contract, traders said.
Diminished concerns about flood damage to the U.S. wheat crop also limited gains.
Talk circulated last week that flooding in the Ohio River Valley could harm the wheat crop there but agronomists Friday said very little wheat would be damaged.
There were expectations for 14 million to 17 million bushels.
Wheat ended 1-1/2 to 3-3/4 cents a bushel higher, with March up 1-1/2 at $3.76-1/2. New crop July closed up three cents at $3.66-1/2.
NYMEX crude sharpened its losses Monday late session as oil prices sagged under ample supplies in the U.S. Gulf and sent prompt crude into a decisive contango, traders said.
"This (contango) could be a temporary blip while the crude is assimilated," said Pat Hughes, market analyst with Chevron Corp in Walnut Creek, Calif.
At 1505 EST, April crude was off 71 cents a barrel at $20.57. April heating oil was off 0.78 cent at 53.30 cents while April gasoline was off 1.37 cent at 64.30 cents a gallon.

New York precious metals ended sharply higher as gold proved resilient enough to stave off further dips below $350.00, and physical demand coupled with comments from a leading fund helped to boost the white metals, traders said.
"In the last couple of trading days gold was unable to get much down past support at $350.00, and silver held its ground quite nicely," analyst Edward Kempf of the CPM group said.
"That's an indication that the troughs in these markets were reached mid-February and prices are having a hard time revisiting them," Kempf added.
COMEX April gold settled $3.20 firmer at $353.10 an ounce, traded $353.30 to $350.80. Later afternoon, bullion was quoted at $351.60/$352.10 an ounce by dealers.

Some traders drew comfort from Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer's comments on Monday that he had heard of no central banks planning gold sales since the Swiss announced their plan last week as a way of raising cash for a new Holocaust fund.
Tietmeyer made his comments following a regular monthly meeting of G-10 central bank governors, of which he is chairman.
Dealers said last week that the gold market's sentiment had been dented by the Swiss plan, coming from a country not expected to sell gold from its central reserves.
